division.heading: Actions Started by Statement of Claim

subdivision.heading: Defence to Statement of Claim, Reply to Defence and Demand for Notice

operative_text.controlling:
3.35(1)  If a lawyer files a statement of defence or demand for
notice on behalf of a defendant, no judgment or order may be
obtained by agreement of the parties unless the defendant’s lawyer
of record is a party to the agreement or consents to the agreement.
(2)  If a defendant
(a) does not file a statement of defence or a demand for
notice,
(b) files a statement of defence or demand for notice in
person or by a lawyer who has ceased to be the
defendant’s lawyer of record, or
(c) is not represented by a lawyer of record,
no judgment or order may be obtained by agreement of the parties
unless the defendant’s agreement, with an affidavit of execution, is
filed with the application for the judgment or order.
(3)  If a lawyer files a statement of claim on behalf of a plaintiff, no
judgment or order may be obtained by agreement of the parties
unless the plaintiff’s lawyer of record is a party to the agreement or
consents to the agreement.
(4)  If a plaintiff
(a) files a statement of claim in person or by a lawyer who
has ceased to be the plaintiff’s lawyer of record, or
(b) is not represented by a lawyer of record,
no judgment or order may be obtained by agreement of the parties
unless the plaintiff’s agreement, with an affidavit of execution, is
filed with the application for the judgment or order.

BOOK_B.title: Judgment or order by agreement

commentary.text: Rule 3.35 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.35. 1. Application of Rule … R. 329 should be read as applying to the time that the consent is endorsed on the proposed judgment or order. If the endorsement and delivery are by the law firm which is then the defendants' solicitor of record, the defendants' later dismissal of that firm, or its later withdrawal, does not nullify the consent. Octa Hage Enterprises Ltd. (314121 Alberta Ltd.) v. Bank of Credit & Commerce Canada (1988), 59 Alta. L.R. (2d) 31 at 32 (C.A.). 2. Approval as to Form Is Not Consent The consent marked on the draft order was “Approved as to form”. It was signed by counsel on behalf of the defendant. I do not regard such a consent or approval as a consent to the substance of the judgment. It purported to be and was, in my opinion, nothing more than an agreement that the draft judgment incorporated the judgment that the trial judge had indicated he would pronounce and was in proper form. It would operate as well, in my opinion, to waive any procedural objection to the motion for the order. Baxter Travenol Laboratories of Canada Ltd. v. Cutter (Canada) Ltd. (1983), 45 N.R. 393 at 424 (Fed. C.A.). 3. Who Is Bound? Consent orders bind only the parties to them. The reality is that this consent order, like most consent orders, is a de facto settlement between the parties to it, which settlement is given judicial sanction. It is a matter of elementary law that A and B cannot agree to something which will adversely affect C's rights. C's agreement is also necessary. Oldham v. Vistula Mobile Home Park Ltd. (1988), 84 A.R. 32 at 48 (Master). 4. Consent Does Not Create Jurisdiction In Morawetz v. Alberta (Director of SafeRoads), 2024 ABKB 588, Justice Marion said: [58] A court cannot grant an order simply because parties present it with a consent order. The order must be something within the jurisdiction and power of the Court, because parties cannot confer jurisdiction to a court by agreement where no jurisdiction exists: Calgary (City) v Bagaric, 2022 ABKB 635 at para 12, citing Transalta Utilities Corporation v Young Estate, 1997 ABCA 349 at para 43; Sedgwick v Edmonton Real Estate Board Co-Operative Listing Bureau Limited (Realtors Association of Edmonton), 2022 ABCA 264; 1658586 Ontario Inc v Can-Am Lubricants Inc, 2014 ONSC 2673 at para 55. 5. Effect of Consent Judgments Although the judgment is a consent judgment, it has the same force and effect as a judgment after trial. Wensel v. Wensel, [1976] 2 W.W.R. 267 (Alta. T.D.), at 270, per Quigley J., affirmed, [1977] 1 W.W.R. 32 (Alta. C.A.). 6. Setting Aside Consent Judgment A consent judgment is not lightly to be set aside. To do so in our view would involve proof of it having been obtained by fraud or deceit. There is no element of that here. L. (D.P.) v. E. (P.A.) (1984), 60 A.R. 87 at 88 (C.A.). On the same topic, Madam Justice Kent said in Schettle v. Lavallee (1994), 153 A.R. 235 (Q.B.), at p. 236: Here, a consent judgment was signed and entered. I am bound by our Court of Appeal in Wensel, Re, [1977] 1 W.W.R. 32 … which held that once a consent judgment is signed by a Queen's Bench judge, as was done here, that judge or any judge with concurrent jurisdiction is functus officio. The only remedy that is available is an appeal of the judgment on the basis that the judgment was obtained by fraud or mistake. That would be for the Court of Appeal to decide. In Dizes v. Dizes (1999), 240 A.R. 14 (Q.B.), Deyell J. came to the same conclusion. An application was made to vacate a consent order (on the allegation that counsel had not been instructed to consent to the order). His Lordship, at p. 15, said: I am bound by our Court of Appeal decision in Wenzel v. Wenzel[sic], [1977] 1 W.W.R. 32 … which held that once a consent judgment is signed by a Queen's Bench judge, that judge or any other Queen's Bench judge is functus officio. The procedure that should have been followed by Timothy Dizes was to appeal the order of Justice Fruman. In Rozinsky v. Rozinsky, 2013 ABCA 113, 2013 CarswellAlta 370, 544 A.R. 334, 82 Alta. L.R. (5th) 344 the Applicant sought to set aside a consent desk divorce judgment on the basis that the Applicant had never instructed his then counsel to consent to it. At paragraphs 6–8, and 10-11, the Court said: [6] There is some authority for the proposition that a consent judgment, having the same force and effect as a judgment after trial, can only be set aside in exceptional circumstances such as fraud, deceit and mutual mistake. See for example the judgment of this Court in D.P.L. v. P.A.E. (1984), 60 A.R. 87. That case, however, did not consider the situation where counsel acted without authority. [7] We appreciate that a lawyer is presumed to have ostensible or apparent authority to settle a claim which he has been retained to commence or defend. Lawyers acting within the scope of their ostensible authority bind their clients even if they are acting without actual authority: Correia v. Danyluk, 2001 ABCA 148, 286 A.R. 117 at para. 11. [8] There is no suggestion on this record that the Respondent had any basis to conclude that the Appellant's then lawyer did not have actual authority to consent to the Ross Judgment. This appearance of actual authority, however, is not dispositive of this appeal. … [10] Even without the Respondent counsel's concession that the Macleod Order was interim in nature, we note that agreements pertaining to custody and access are not binding upon the Court. It is open to the Court in an appropriate case (for example, where counsel acted without actual authority in defiance of his client's instructions) to refuse to decide such issues finally and definitively in the context of a divorce judgment. See Stewart v. Stewart (1990), 112 A.R. 137 (C.A.). In the case at bar, Court approval is a condition precedent to resolving the corollary relief prayed for in the Ross Judgment. [11] Having concluded that the Appellant's instruction to former counsel to appeal the Macleod Order constitutes, in effect, directions not to agree to the Ross Judgment and its corollary relief, and mindful that the Court's intervention was necessary to carry out the agreement to proceed to a divorce judgment in circumstances where the Appellant's former counsel acted in defiance of express instructions, appellate relief is appropriate. 7. Interpreting a consent order In Cho v. Harmony Ceramic Dental Laboratory Ltd., 2024 ABKB 571, a dispute arose over the interpretation of an order which had been granted on consent. The question came back before Justice Jeffrey who had granted the consent order, but he noted, in paragraph 3, that “[a]ll judges are equally positioned to interpret a consent order's meaning and application.” Justice Jeffrey set out the approach to be taken in interpreting a consent order's meaning. His Lordship said: [4] A consent order results from the parties to it reaching their own agreement. The interpretation of a consent order, therefore, is not an inquiry into what the signing judge meant by the wording of the order. [5] The interpretation of a consent order follows the same approach as the interpretation of any other form of agreement between private parties. The Alberta Court of Appeal summarized that approach in Canadian Natural Resources Limited v Wood Group Mustang (Canada) Inc. (IMV Projects Inc.), 2018 ABCA 305, at para 97: The objective of contractual interpretation is to ascertain the intention of the contracting parties by reading the contract as a whole, giving the words used their ordinary and grammatical meaning, consistent with the surrounding circumstances known to the parties at the time of the formation of the contract. The words of any one provision must not be read in isolation but should be considered in harmony with the rest of the contract and in light of its purposes and … context: Ledcor Construction Ltd. v Northbridge Indemnity Insurance Co., 2016 SCC 37 at para. 27, [2016] 2 SCR 23; Tercon Contractors Ltd. v British Columbia (Transportation and Highways), 2010 SCC 4 at para. 64, [2010] 1 SCR 69. [6] I found additional guidance on the interpretation of agreements in the form of consent orders from the following authorities: Shell Canada Products v Sunterra Beef Ltd, 2016 ABCA 250; Larcencova v Makarenko, 2018 ABCA 417; and Custom Metal Installations Ltd v Winspia Windows (Canada) Inc, 2020 ABCA 333. The Consent Order here is what the Alberta Court of Appeal calls an “interlocutory procedural consent order”, not a “final consent order”: see Custom Metal Installations, at paras 42 to 59.
